beats: Your freezer turns on a heater. A few times a day. On purpose.
It hides behind the back wall, under a coil covered in frost.
That coil is the evaporator, the part that actually makes the cold.
Every time you open the door, moist air rushes in and freezes onto it.
Frost insulates the coil and clogs its gaps. The fan can't push cold air through.
So a timer steps in. It stops the compressor and the fan.
Then the heater under the coil switches on: around five hundred watts.
A small thermostat on the coil cuts it at five Celsius, forty-one Fahrenheit.
The melted frost runs down a tube into a tray sitting on the compressor.
The compressor's warmth evaporates it, back into your kitchen air.
The whole defrost takes well under an hour, too short to thaw your food.
Frost-free just means your freezer melts its own frost, on a schedule.
